I’ll check the project and attached photo for the Arduino and driver details, then write the motor test code using the firmware skill.
The project records an Uno, CNC Shield V3, and A4988 drivers. I’m making a slow continuous-spin sketch with start/stop commands; the shield’s axis socket determines which pins it needs.

The photo shows four installed drivers, so the sketch will let you choose X, Y, or Z with a command such as `START X`. It will spin until `STOP` and stay stopped after reset. I’m also using the owned-parts intake skill to attach the photo to the existing records.
The sketch compiles successfully for the Uno and uses 16.1% of RAM. No board is currently detected over USB, so it has not been flashed or tested on the motor.

Created the [motor-spin sketch](<control/continuous_spin/continuous_spin.ino>). **Compiled successfully for Arduino Uno.**

1. Upload it with `mechy_control.h` beside it.
2. Open Serial Monitor: **115200 baud**, **Newline**.
3. Send `START X`—use `Y` or `Z` if that’s your motor’s socket.
4. Send `STOP` to stop.

It ramps to **200 step pulses/second** and spins continuously. It stays stopped after reset.

Not hardware-tested. The shield enables all drivers together; an A socket configured to mirror your chosen axis will also move. [Setup instructions](<docs/continuous-spin.md>).
Did you make the changes to run the motor on A
The current sketch only supports X, Y, and Z. I’ll check the A-axis routing before adding it.
A support was missing. I’m adding `START A` using D12 for STEP and D13 for DIR, then rebuilding. The shield must route A to those pins; its jumper configuration is still unverified.

**Added A support now**—it was missing before. The [updated sketch](</Users/Carlo/Empire/Projects/BAM/Imported Arm Projects/Mechy Demo/control/continuous_spin/continuous_spin.ino>) compiles successfully for Uno.

1. With power disconnected, configure A for independent **D12 STEP / D13 DIR** routing. [Shield guide](https://makerhardware.net/wiki/doku.php?id=electronics:cnc_shield)
2. Upload the updated sketch.
3. Open Serial Monitor at **115200 baud**, **Newline**, and send `START A`.
4. Send `STOP` to stop.

The actual jumper routing remains unverified. I haven’t uploaded it or tested the motor.

I'm mapping the current base and the upper-arm hardware before I redesign the base housing and add the missing pulleys, belts, bearings and screws.
Status: I've mapped every bore in the arm's printed parts. Next I'm designing the enclosed base housing and generating the belts, bearings, axles and screws at those bores.
Status: geometry mapped. Now writing the new base housing, bearing cover, and a hardware generator (belts, bearings, axles, screws, nuts).
Status: new base housing and bearing cover build as valid solids. Now writing the hardware generator for belts, bearings and fasteners.
Status: build script updated (new base, real bearing/screw models, belts, upper hardware, BOM counts). Running the build now.
Status: first hardware screen flagged many contacts; checking whether that's a real placement error or a flaw in the screening method.
Status: seat and screw fixes applied. Adding penetration-depth measurement to the screen so contacts and real clashes are separated.
Status: hardware screen passes with 0 interferences (belts clear everything). Running the full base assembly, print and regression checks.
Status: base checks now show 0 interferences and every printed part slices; the only flags are the known 0.1 mm coupling-screw gaps. Running the motion and hardware screens.
Status: new cover and housing pass wall checks; the only overhangs left are the planned counterbore bridges. Rebuilding and re-running every check.
Now the build plan, bearing model record and summary text.
Status: cover reworked (screws inside the collar, nothing outside r38.5). Nudging the bosses for wall margin, then the full rebuild and checks.
Status: waiting on the motion screen; meanwhile the report text is updated for the final cover design.
Looks right. Waiting for the motion screen to finish before the final rebuild.
Motion screen is clean (0 penetrations in 27 poses). Running the final rebuild, checks, hardware screen and report.

I replaced the table-like base with an enclosed round housing, and the CAD now shows belts on the pulleys plus every bearing, axle, screw and nut ([iso view](design/bam-v2/views/iso.png), [base close-up](design/bam-v2/views/base_iso.png), [exploded base](design/bam-v2/views/base_exploded.png)).

1. **Base:** The motor is now walled in on all sides, with vent slots, a cable port for the motor plug and a foot ring for bench screws. A closed cover replaces the four-post retainer. It's one part instead of the old open stand, it prints without supports, and it sliced successfully.
2. **Pulleys and hardware:** The two big "gears" on the arm are actually belt pulleys, so I added both belts. I also added 9 missing bearings, M6/M4 pivot bolts with nuts, and the motor, bracket and gripper screws. Five existing bearings were mislabeled, so I renamed them. The [BOM](design/bam-v2/bom.csv) shows how many of each item the CAD models.
3. **Checks run:** The base parts have no interferences at four yaw angles. The new hardware doesn't clash with the arm (belts touch nothing), and 27 sampled arm poses don't hit the base. The only flags are expected screw-thread contacts and the two coupling screws already sitting at the 0.1 mm clearance limit. During checking I fixed real problems: a cover opening that hit the turntable, endstop screws that hit the motor-screw heads (now M3x5), and a cover that hit the arm at an extreme pose.

Still open:
- With the shoulder at 15° and the elbow fully folded, the forearm passes only about 0.9 mm above the base edge. That needs a firmware limit before anyone runs moves at the joint limits.
- The old mismatch is still there: the CAD shows 20T motor pulleys but the settings assume 16T.
- Yaw homing is still unresolved, and the new base needs 4 M3 heat-set inserts.
- I haven't run the print release check, so none of this is ready to print or order yet. Details are in the [summary](design/bam-v2/summary.md).
Make the gripper better. Look at online designs for reference
I’ll inspect the current gripper, research online mechanisms, and use the printable-part, industrial-design, and assembly skills to improve it.

The active BAM model uses an MG996R-size servo, while older project notes mention an MG90S. I’m checking the actual CAD mounting points so the upgrade matches the arm you’re viewing. The references point toward parallel jaws and replaceable soft pads for more consistent contact.

I found a real inconsistency: the viewer shows the original stepper-driven gripper, but the print list specifies a servo version. I’ll correct that mismatch while improving the fingers and adding replaceable TPU pads. The existing jaw guides can be reused.

The original mechanism already keeps the jaws parallel. I’m retaining that motion and replacing the short, thin gripping ends with longer, reinforced fingers and removable TPU pads. I’m also correcting the servo carrier’s mounting holes, which were about 1 mm off the wrist holes.

The new fingers and pads are modeled. The first print check caught thin features inherited from the old guides, so I’m correcting those before release. The pads have flat gripping areas and a shallow groove for round objects; their fasteners sit below the contact surface.

The servo carrier and drive hardware now pass their interference screen. I’m checking the complete gripper next; that caught contacts between the new pads and retained finger geometry, which I’m removing. Servo and horn fit still depend on measurements of the actual MG90S.
Codex usage limit reached. Send a message after it resets to continue; the session resumes.

I’ll give the gripper a cleaner silhouette: a protective servo cover, tapered jaws, recessed hardware, and a consistent dark finish with contrasting grip pads.
